cells.tense: Something in front of you hasn't been forced shut yet, and your hands on it are steady.
cells.ask: Give one thing that's still taking shape a hand today — a lift, a meal, an hour — and then let it be without asking anyone how it went.
cells.core:
You're looking after something that hasn't decided what it's going to be. Not rushing it into a name, not demanding it prove itself before it's ready. You feed it, shape it a little, give it room — and that's what lets a possibility survive contact with the world instead of dying in the open. Holding a thing open while it forms is a real skill, and most people don't have it.

None of this is free. You stay answerable for something you can't finish yet, and open things need watching even when no one can see you doing it. The watching can be done with a loose hand, though — steady, unhurried, yours. Nothing here needs to be proven today.
cells.sheetLine: You're giving it shape without forcing it into a name.
cells.verb: Tending what's growing with steady hands, giving it the shape it needs and letting it take its time.
cells.place: The wide-open place before anything has been settled — everything still possible, nothing committed yet.

cells.tense: You're already living several steps ahead, arranging things now for a version of this that hasn't shown up.
cells.ask: Write one honest picture of this finished — just for you — then close the notebook and do nothing with it today.
cells.core:
You hold a picture of what the thing could become and let that picture inform your hands without deciding for it. You can see the shape and still let the shape surprise you — that's the working version, and it's rare. The trouble starts when the picture gets so specific the real thing can't match it, and you begin managing an outcome you can't reach. Planning is useful. Planning can't hand you the result.

What you're bracing against is unfinished, not ruined. The slow, ordinary version — the one forming while you're not watching — is the one with somewhere to go. Standing over it won't speed it up; it'll only cost you the view. Put the picture on paper and it stops governing the room.
cells.sheetLine: You're minding a thing that hasn't arrived yet.
cells.verb: Tending what's growing with steady hands, giving it the shape it needs and letting it take its time.
cells.place: The wide-open place before anything has been settled — everything still possible, nothing committed yet.

cells.tense: You're at a door that's already behind you, still looking back at what you didn't choose.
cells.ask: Pick one real thing you've made in the last year — a repair, a meal, a sentence — and tell one person it's done.
cells.core:
Watching over a possibility can be a light hand — water it on the days you notice it, leave it alone on the days you don't, and the timing doesn't worry you. That ease has gone quiet lately. The wide-open part of this feels like a room you don't walk into, so you wait for something to be certain first — and things only get certain by being tended. Nothing gets there by waiting for the certainty to show up on its own.

What's past isn't a verdict. It's unfinished, and unfinished isn't spoiled. A seed that stopped getting water is still a seed, and it takes water whenever it's offered. That's the whole ask — small, real, doable today. Whether it grows isn't promised, only that the ground is still yours.
cells.sheetLine: You've stopped watering it, and it's still a seed.
cells.verb: Tending what's growing with steady hands, giving it the shape it needs and letting it take its time.
cells.place: The wide-open place before anything has been settled — everything still possible, nothing committed yet.

cells.tense: You're already holding this open — it shows in how you spend your days — but you talk about it like the situation is doing it.
cells.ask: Tell one person, plainly, that you've been keeping this open on purpose, and use your own words for what you're doing.
cells.core:
Look at what's still undecided around you and you'll find your hand on it. You keep doors open, you give things room, you let a possibility stay possible because it isn't ready to be anything else — that's care, and it's work, deliberate work. Calling it just the way things are takes the credit off the one who's doing it. That credit belongs to you, and it's real.

None of this is costless. Care with no end date is heavy, and saying it out loud means it can be looked at, maybe even paused. But naming it doesn't lock it down. It lets the keeping-open stop pretending it isn't happening — and lets you keep doing it on purpose.

attempts.check: The record gives this card, this seat and this status; it does not say what the person has tried, what it cost, or who else is involved, so the draft must stay at the level of the capacity, not a story about it. A reader could fairly say that keeping an option open is sometimes the right move and that a narrow decision can be a mistake, so the ask must stay an experiment that commits nothing. The ask survives — writing and setting one opening line aside teaches the person something about whether they actually want to take it — but any sentence that tells them what they've been avoiding or what they'll feel would serve me more than them. Cut anything that names a person's history or motive; keep only what the capacity looks like in this part of a life.
